author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Rural communities face continuing violence amid militarization
content:
Photo by Viggo Sarmago/Bulatlat

Under the blazing sun in front Camp Aguinaldo, palay hats stood out together with the line of banners. It was not a celebration for peasants — but a plea to end militarization, violence, and to serve justice for Negros 19 killed in Toboso, Negros Occidental on April 19, 2026.

Farmers and fisherfolk play a vital role in sustaining the nation’s food security and economy, yet they are the ones who struggle the most to survive.

Pamalakaya’s National Vice Chairperson Ronnel Arambulo stated in his speech during the fourth day of peasant month protest on October 19, that the administration does not aim to protect the life and rights of the people, farmers, and fisherfolk, but to protect the ruling class, the foreigners, and the people in power for their own personal interest.

Fisherfolks are also facing harassment that disrupts their lives. According to Arambulo, there are recent reports of intimidation in Binangonan, Rizal, where fisherfolk were called by Maritime Police to appear at the municipal hall. They were later summoned to renounce and abandon Pamalakaya.

This kind of intimidation is not confined to the province of Rizal, as similar deployments have also been reported in other regions.

Nida Barcenas from Karapatan-Bicol stated that the 9th Infantry “Spear” Division of Philippine Army or at least ten battalions of men in uniform were scattered around six provinces in Bicol region.

During the “Stakeholder and Media Fellowship Night: Episode 1 – Kaakibat sa Kapayapaan,” event of 9th Infantry Division held on April 18, 2026 at Camp Elias Angeles, Maj. Gen. Aldwine I. Almase recognized the efforts of national agencies, local government units, media personalities, and other stakeholders in countering alleged local terrorist activities to ensure peace and safety in the Bicol region.

For Karapatan-Bicol , however, these achievements actually meant human rights abuses against farmers communities. As of March 2026, Karapatan has recorded 46 political prisoners in Bicol — 9 of them are women, with 22 arrested under Marcos Jr. administration. In his four year term in the government, two enforced disappearances and 38 extrajudicial killings have also been documented.

Red-tagging, violence, and land grabbing continue to disrupt the lives of Bicolanos, Barcenas said.

“To this day, residents of Masbate continue to appeal for help amid alleged land grabbing by Governor Kho. Farmers are being driven off their lands, and those who resist are killed and red-tagged as NPAs, [New People’s Army]” Barcenas said.

The issue involving Governor Antonio Kho is also part of the problem regarding land dispute over the Pecson Estate in Cawayan, Masbate. Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) stated that Kho took over a portion of 1,807-hectare estate, forcing more than 100 farmers off the lands they have cultivated for years.

The agrarian conflict has also been associated with reports of killing involving peasants in Cawayan. A human rights report from Karapatan revealed cases including killings of farmers named Pancho Versaga and Renard Remulta on October 28, 2022 in Sitio Villaluna, Barangay Itom-Bato, Cawayan. These two were among more than 100 farmers tilling a 450-hectare portion of the Pecson Estate within land seized by Kho in Masbate.

Karapatan has declared Masbate as Bicol’s killing fields due to an increasing number of victims who had been killed under Marcos Jr. regime’s counter-insurgency war on the province.

One of the heinous cases was the killing of a farmer couple Aimee and Jover Villegas, a two-hectare land caretaker. The military said that the couple died under armed encounters. However, their injuries contradict this claim as Aimee’s throat, chin, and neck had been slashed, while Jover sustained gunshot wounds in the nape and back.

Echoing this concern, Grace Nabian from Amihan-Negros called for a stop to the militarization in rural communities.

She questioned killings, abduction, and threats against farmers, stressing that land reform, and access to quality education for their children are what they need.

She also pressed his demand to hold Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) accountable for various deaths in their land including Negros 19.

During an afternoon mass in a collective protest campout in front of the Department of Agrarian Reform, Sol Santuyo, mother of Maureen Santuyo, emphasized the long-overdue demand of farmers that were ignored by the government.

“From then until now, our farmers have had one cry, but those in power deliberately turn a deaf ear. I hope a better way is found, so that no more youth would have to risk their lives just to help our farmers,” Santuyo, whose daughter was among those killed in Toboso, said.

Various organizations along with other student activists continue to call for justice for Santuyo, Alyssa Alano, RJ Ledesma, and Errol Wendell, Lyle Prijoles, Kai Sorem, and others but to all farmers, fisherfolk, journalists, and residents who were killed, abducted, threatened, and deprived of land and rights. (RVO)

author: Shannia Cabuello
title: Molbog community exposes agenda behind land-use projects
content:
They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds.

“They want to take everything so we insisted on coming here to express ourselves. We will embrace our land even if they harass us. We will not give it even if we get hurt.”

Molbog community member Anjilon Flores from Balabac Palawan stressed this point as Molbog indigenous peoples travelled to Metro Manila ahead of US President Donald Trump’s visit.

They aim to amplify their resistance against the Department of Environmental and Natural Resources’ Enhanced National Greening Program (E-NGP) and the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA).

Along with multi-sectoral groups and environmental advocates, they exposed the E-NGP and EDCA as tools of imperialist war and resource plunder, threatening the life, livelihood, culture, and ancestral lands of the Molbog people.

Long before Spanish colonial rule, the Molbog community have been the traditional stewards of Balabac island, depending on coconut farming, shifting cultivation, fishing, and harvesting seaweeds for livelihood.

“Palawan is a key biodiversity area and known to be the last ecological frontier of the Philippines,” Bianca Intia of Kalikasan Timog Katagalugan (TK) said at a press conference on October 26.

It shelters several endemic animal and plant species, including Philippine Mouse-deer which are exclusively found in Balabac and nearby islands.

Flores described their fields as prosperous with cassava, banana, corn, peanuts, and rice, making it their community’s main source of income for decades.

For them, lands are sacred that require ancestral permission before undertaking any activities like when entering the land, performing rituals, planting, harvesting, and cutting trees.

Born in Balabac, Flores cannot accept the prohibitions imposed by the E-NGP in using their resources. “They would restrict us from cutting trees which we use for firewood. This is also the livelihood for most of us. What will happen if they forbid us? Our livelihood will also be gone.”

Bangsa Molbog leader Emmanuel San Esteban lamented the encroachment of Balabac Air Base on their homes, sacred prayer grounds, and burial sites in Barangay Catagupan without any consultation with their tribal officials.

“They turned our ancestor’s burial sites into dumping grounds. The mountains where we do our rituals were flattened,” San Esteban said.

The local authorities said that the remains of their ancestors would be transferred to a different location. However, this is against the principles and culture of the Molbog tribe.

The indigenous residents dread the impact of both projects, as it begins to disrupt their peace, routines, and tradition.

They stressed that access to their land has been restricted, limiting the products they could gather from the forest.

According to DENR, the E-NGP was signed to rehabilitate the estimated 1.2 million hectares of the remaining unproductive, denuded, and degraded forestlands by 2022. It also aimed to maintain and protect existing forests.

This was already implemented by the DENR in several areas in Balabac where trees were planted in Barangay Catagupan, Agutayan, and Indalawan.

The communities worried about fines for damaging plants under E-NGP while clearing farmland. Cutting a tree must also be replaced with a hundred more trees and a Php 6,000 ($94) fine.

Kalikasan TK underscored that E-NGP did not aim to benefit communities but only to carbon offset the Ipilan Nickel Corporation’s deforestation and mining operations in Brooke’s Point, Palawan.

The Molbog people also expressed concerns that monocropping and fast-growing plant species under the E-NGP could affect forest biodiversity and native vegetation.

“The E-NGP is within our ancestral domain, for which we had applied for a Certificate on Ancestral Domain Title (CADT),” said San Esteban, questioning how the project progressed faster than their CADT application.

They first filed their CADT application in 2004 but the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) only certified the application in 2019. To expedite the process, the NCIP required them to pay at least Php 1.6 million ($25,092.33). Their CADT remains pending.

San Esteban said that Balabac Air Base in Barangay Catagupan also pushed through because of the NCIP’s manipulation of the Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) process.

“Our mayor has been conducting surveys in our area. Only eight people agreed to the project while the majority of more than 100 said no,” San Esteban said. The NCIP conducted similar surveys in other areas and used the results to support documents for the project’s approval.

Earlier this year, the Southern Tagalog Exposure (STeX), along with environmental defenders, visited Balabac to investigate the project’s impacts. It would be built along Molbog’s 26,000 hectares of ancestral domain and waters, specifically in Barangay Catagupan with a population of 2,000 people.

Marky Casaquite of STeX said that residents believe that a headquarters building would be ready in around two months. Some of those who are living on the land were hired for the EDCA site construction with a promise of a stable job. They later learned that they would only be employed for this specific facility.

Since its construction, residents have also reported incidents of physical assault and violence inflicted by municipal and military officers.

“I am the one being targeted by the soldiers wearing facial coverings. They do not introduce themselves when they threaten me,” San Esteban said.

When he raised their concerns about road restrictions to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), San Esteban experienced being kicked in the back by municipal officers. He tried issuing a blotter but the police declined to document the incident.

“So you know, if something happened to me, they are the ones to blame. They said straight to my face that they will soften my head and dump it somewhere,” he said.

San Esteban also criticized the unannounced live military exercises that sowed fear among their children. Foreign military soldiers were also being deployed in their area.

“The children are being scared. They were covering their ears because they did not inform our community that they would fire their guns,” he said in an interview.

According to the Balabac Air Station’s Base Development Plan, the EDCA site would cover approximately 301 hectares of land for 45 facilities that include firing range, solar farm, solar power plant, and Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR) Hangar.

The Hangar would serve as aircraft staging and maintenance, logistical sortie and distribution hub, and civil military coordination center.

Earlier this year, the US army brought a rocket launcher to Balabac Island to conduct a temporary live fire simulation. Molbog people were aware of the ongoing conflict between the US and China, but contested that it is not enough basis to use ancestral lands for war.

“I hope those foreigners will be expelled from our lands. Since they got here, all they brought are restrictions and deception,” San Esteban said.

“The destruction of Balabac, Palawan is multifaceted in cause and consequence. The construction of the EDCA air base and the implementation of the E-NGP prioritize US strategic and corporate interest over the welfare of the Molbog community and the environment,” Intia said in a statement.

National Coordinator of Bai Indigenous Women’s Network Kim Falyao stressed that these are also experienced by the locals in Dupax Del Norte and Kasibu due to large-scale minings, the Igorot due to renewable energy projects, the Tumandok due to Jalaur Mega Dam, and the Ayta due to the Pax Silica Initiative.

“Marcos Jr. markets our lands as sources of minerals and wealth that serves the greed of the United States, building Philippine and US bases, camps, and facilities where they store weapons and conduct military exercises,” said Falyao, condemning the militarization that only threatens, bombs, and protects these projects.

Mong Palatino of Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) said that these aggressive developments in critical ecosystems are global preparations for imperialist war and plunder.

“Stop land grabbing, investigate those who inflict violence, and put them in jail. We hope the soldiers will be removed from our area so they can no longer disturb us,” San Esteban said.

On the approaching visit of US President Donald Trump, Falyao said that Indigenous Peoples would reiterate their calls to drive away the greedy US imperialist that plunders, destroys the environment, and kills the Indigenous Peoples lives and livelihood.

“Hope is not lost. The Filipino people are not afraid to express their indignation. Witness this on Trump’s visit to the Philippines during the ASEAN Summit,” Palatino said. (RTS, DAA)

title: Women on the frontlines defending land, life, and livelihood
content:
Across the Philippines, one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries, women are at the forefront of struggles to defend their communities against displacement, environmental destruction, and development aggression. From the mountains of Luzon to the coastal communities of the Visayas and Mindanao, they are fighting to protect the land and resources that make life possible.

In Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya, about 300 women are actively involved in a long-running struggle against large-scale mining. They help maintain six community barricades that have blocked mining operations since 2007. Among the companies seeking to operate in the area is North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC), whose government-issued exploration permit covers 4,456 hectares of land, threatening farms and watersheds that sustain thousands of residents. Click here to read their story.

Further south, the struggle takes a different form. In Tacloban, elderly women are protecting the coastal community they rebuilt after super typhoon Yolanda (international name: Haiyan) in 2013. The typhoon destroyed most of the area’s two-hectare mangrove forest, reducing it to just 2,000 square meters. Two months after Yolanda, they joined other residents in growing seedlings and restoring the mangroves of Cancabato Bay. title: Women tending the Kasibu barricades against large-scale mining
content:
At the barricade, she has found her place by turning its often-invisible work of care into a collective act of resistance.







KASIBU, Nueva Vizcaya – In this third class municipality some 300 kilometers north of Luzon, land is life. It feeds families, sustains Indigenous communities, and carries generations of history. Yet under Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s banner of “development,” mining expansion threatens to dispossess communities of the very land that keeps them alive. 




In defense of their land, the people of Kasibu set up the people’s barricade against large-scale mining. Their steadfastness was met with force when on

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Grieving without graves
content:
Families of enforced disappearance victims gather in a mass, offering tribute to their loved ones. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

The commemoration of All Souls Day may be different for the loved ones of enforced disappearance victims (desaparecidos) but their annual gathering is a symbol of determination in their continuous search.

“We gather here together because we don’t have a grave to mourn at,” said Edith Burgos, vice chairperson of Karapatan and president of International Coalition Against Enforced Disappearances (ICAED).

Burgos is the mother of Jonas Burgos, a farmer-activist who was forcibly disappeared on April 28, 2007 at Ever Gotesco Mall, Quezon City. For almost two decades, she has been active in campaigning to surface Jonas and other desaparecidos.

“It might not be now, but I am sure that we will see justice. That even just a few of our loved ones will finally surface. There is zero success (rate) in searching for the disappeared here in the Philippines. Our hope remains,” Burgos said.

Some of the families have been searching for more than four decades, since the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr., father of the current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

“My parents and my siblings died without seeing the body of my brother (Levi), without justice,” said Xcy Ybañez, brother of Cebu-based activist Rolando “Levi” Ybañez who was forcibly disappeared on July 11, 1985. On that same day, Redemptorist priest Fr. Rosaleo “Rudy” Romano was also forcibly disappeared by military agents.

Spanning administrations from Marcos Sr. to Marcos Jr., Karapatan and Desaparecidos documented at least 1,900 victims who had never surfaced as of this writing. While there is a law that criminalizes enforced disappearance, there has been no successful prosecution.

“Grieving is the processing of the loss of our loved ones,” said Ligaya Portajada, wife of labor activist Armando Portajada Sr. who was forcibly disappeared on July 14, 1988. “But for us in Desaparecidos, our grief and sorrow are never-ending, not until the surfacing of our loved ones. I wish for this crime to stop. Our loved ones are not criminals, they are only helping the marginalized people.”

Portajada Sr. was the Coca-Cola workers’ union president when he was abducted. Human rights defenders like him are often the target of enforced disappearance, affecting not only their families but also the communities they serve.

“Dad loves his family and friends. But most of all, he loves the people of Cordillera,” said Gabrielle Chuwaley Capuyan, daughter of indigenous rights activist Dexter Capuyan who was forcibly disappeared together with Gene Roz Jamil “Bazoo” De Jesus on April 28, 2023. “He chose to offer his strength to serve the indigenous peoples and farmers of Cordillera.”

Capuyan recalled that the communities they visited to find her father’s whereabouts is the reason to hold on to hope: Dexter was described as youthful, always ready to help, finding comfort in watching sitcoms, laughing amusely, with a dimple and posture resembling a certain actor from the series Boys Over Flowers. “It never fails to make us smile.”

Dexter and Bazoo were among the recent victims under the current administration. A year after, two other activists disappeared, namely veteran labor organizer James Jazmines and environmental activist Felix Salaveria Jr.

Their families filed petitions for writ of amparo and habeas data. On August 12, 2025, the Court of Appeals (CA) declared Dexter and Bazoo as victims of enforced disappearance, contrary to the outcome of the police investigation. Similarly, writs of amparo were also issued to Jazmines and Salaveria last year

Desaparecidos Philippines wrote to the Supreme Court (SC) to review the writs of amparo and habeas data for its “persistent ineffectiveness” for nearly two decades, without a single success story.

Read: Not one surfaced despite court orders, families demand review of legal remedies

“The government agencies, who were supposed to find our father, had shown us their apathy and incompetence. It is as if not a single life is at stake,” said Salaveria’s eldest daughter Felicia Ferrer. “Is there value to the decision of the Courts, if until now, my father has not yet surfaced? When justice remains elusive for all our fathers, mothers, children, and loved ones?”

Since the court orders did not result in the surfacing of their loved ones, Burgos earlier flagged that the process is long when it’s supposed to be a “swift” remedy. She said that state forces are uncooperative and hostile to the families and that there is no thorough investigation despite orders from the court. She added that no one is cited in contempt for not following.

More than 100 families, friends, and advocates gathered during the mass, followed by a short symbolic program to honor the desaparecidos as white roses were tied to the portraits of the victims and their names were recited.

“They frequently told us to move on and accept it as it is,” said Desaparecidos chairperson JL Burgos, filmmaker and brother of Jonas. “But how can we accept it if our questions remain unanswered, our loved ones remain missing, and without justice?”

While enforced disappearance is defined as a state-perpetrated or state-sanctioned crime, JL said that perpetrators are shielded by an impenetrable shroud of impunity. It is this impunity, he said, that is behind the fact that enforced disappearances continue to this day.

He called on the Philippine government to enforce the Anti-Enforced Disappearance Law. He also urged for the ratification of the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, the only core international human rights treaty that the Philippines has not yet ratified.

“With the government dead set on denying us the truth, the November 2 gathering is ultimately an act of defiance,” JL said. “We declare that we have not forgotten our missing loved ones, we have not stopped searching for the truth behind their disappearance and calling for them to be surfaced, and we will not yield to the state’s attempts to threaten, harass or intimidate us.” (RTS, DAA)

author: Maverick Avila
title: ‘Long fight ahead after ethanol spill in Tañon Strait’ – lawyer in landmark case
content:
Wastewater from an ethanol spill discolors Bais Bay, the Philippines’ Negros Oriental province, on Oct. 28, 2025, days after ethanol wastewater spilled into the bay, causing significant damage to coastal and marine ecosystems. Image courtesy of MarGale Bancairen.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX).

In 2007, Philippine environmental lawyer Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio and four other law professors in Cebu City sat around laughing at an idea: representing marine mammals in court.

Despite the somewhat funny concept, they were serious about their goal: Stop the oil exploration in the Tañon Strait by Japan Petroleum Exploration (JAPEX). The protected seascape between the islands of Cebu and Negros is home to 14 whale and dolphin species, as well as coral reefs and mangrove forests. The Japanese energy company performed seismic surveys and drilled an exploration well, which drove away dolphins and whales from the strait.

It was an ambitious plan, as animals had never been named as petitioners. Eisma-Osorio and fellow lawyer Golly Estenzo Ramos filed the first petition representing the resident marine mammals in December 2007. Their colleagues filed a second petition on behalf of fishing communities directly affected by the exploration activities.

The case, Resident Marine Mammals of the Protected Seascape Tañon Strait v. Secretary Angelo Reyes, went on for several years. In April 2015, the Philippine Supreme Court ruled to void the contract that allowed the exploration, development, and exploitation of petroleum resources within the Tañon Strait.

Eisma-Osorio joined Oceana Philippines as a consultant in 2015, a year after the NGO was established. At 56, she now leads the campaign and legal department as senior director of Oceana Philippines.

On October 24, 2025, a major ethanol wastewater spill hit Bais Bay, part of the Tañon Strait Protected Seascape (TSPS). Oceana Philippines collaborated with marine scientists to assess the severity of the spill. Their research, with the latest report in July this year, found that Universal Robina Corporation’s (URC) ethanol plant continued to leak wastewater, killing fish, corals and seagrass. The NGO is also consulting with fishing communities to build a court case against the company.

With more than 25 years of experience in natural resources law and policy, Eisma-Osorio believes it’s her personal responsibility to ensure there is legal accountability. In an interview with Mongabay via video call, she talked about representing marine mammals, the reaction from the community, and her current legal fight.

Mongabay: What was your thought process in deciding to represent the marine mammals in such a landmark case?

Rose Liza Eisma-Osorio: It was an ambitious undertaking. We wanted to challenge the thinking that only humans can file cases in court. And we knew there were two ways it could go: the court would throw out the case or decide to hear it. So we wanted to be sure, and we had Attorney Ramos and myself to act as stewards representing the marine mammals.

If you look at the case caption, the marine mammals were joined and represented by us, meaning they were also signing as individuals while being represented by us, because if the court did not allow them to join as litigants, it could still allow us to represent the dolphins and whales.

Mongabay: How was the case received back then, by communities, environmental groups, and even the court?

Eisma-Osorio: Around that time, what was refreshing about the campaign was that there was already an organic movement, especially the Save Tañon Strait Movement. There were very active Cebuanos, individuals, and students who helped raise awareness. The fisherfolk we represented were part of it too, so there was community engagement, because we knew they were the injured party in a way.

That was also the strategy behind two petitions. In the Philippines, you have to suffer an injury for the court to say you’re entitled to the remedy. We wanted the fisherfolk to prove their reduced catch and be heard, in the event that the court did not listen to the resident marine mammals case, since proof of injury was still a big question mark at that time.

Mongabay: At what point did you say, ‘This case is winnable?’ What was the turning point in lobbying to represent the resident marine mammals, especially with court updates?

Eisma-Osorio: We didn’t expect it to be in our favor. When we filed it in December 2007, the turning point was that even before the court decided, JAPEX pulled out. That was our early victory.

Then in 2015, the court decided in our favor, which was an added bonus. What the court zeroed in on, and what made it a landmark case, is that you don’t have to show proof of personal injury to represent nature as stewards and give nature legal standing in court. Only that you are here representing nature and this is the damage that was done.

We were surprised, and we said, “OK, we’ve set a precedent in Philippine jurisprudence.” This makes it easier for our citizens to file environmental cases now.

Mongabay: What immediate effect did you see after the Supreme Court decision?

Eisma-Osorio: After we won the case, I became Oceana’s consultant, and we decided to work on the management plan for Tañon Strait, because even if it was established as a protected seascape in 1998, there was no management plan at all.

Our contribution went beyond the case, [we got] into managing the area well and enforcing the laws and rules there. We left a living document that allows the agencies and local governments to work together to manage Tañon Strait in a better way.

Mongabay: Nine months after the October 2025 ethanol spill in Bais Bay, Silliman University marine scientists found the pollution killed up to 69 percent of coral cover in the assessed reef areas. What does it mean for Oceana to lobby again for the community?

Eisma-Osorio: Tañon Strait will always be our legacy campaign. When there are challenges like the ethanol spill, we need to go back and do our part.

We worked with the scientists from Silliman University to elevate the issue into a national concern, and we were pleasantly surprised by how our [press release] became viral. The communications tool is always useful, and it helped move the Department of Environment and Natural Resources. They have filed a criminal action against the responsible officers of URC, and I think the case is now ongoing.

But there’s still the matter of the ongoing leakage that continues to affect the fishing communities. And if it’s not stopped, then it might become worse and turn the bay into a wasteland.

We’re not entirely satisfied, because there are legal tools like the Writ of Kalikasan that could ensure the bay is restored and responsible actors are held accountable.

It’s early days, but there is an opportunity to ensure the community gets the justice it deserves for the damage to their resources and livelihood. Bais Bay is small compared to the entire stretch of Tañon Strait, but it’s ground zero for some because it’s where you do the dolphin and whale watching. If livelihoods are thriving there, you’ve protected Tañon Strait. That’s why it’s my personal quest to ensure environmental justice for what happened in Bais Bay.

Mongabay: Do you think it’s going to be a long battle ahead?

Eisma-Osorio: Yes, it will be a long battle ahead. We will be battling this together with the community. Nothing about them should be without them.

title: Police withdraws from Kasibu as residents stand their ground against mining
content:
Local community maintained the barricade while police forces gear up to dismantle it, Screengrab from Nhe Riz

Alyansa ng Novo Vizcayano para sa Kalikasan (ANVIK) argued that the court should hold NLMRC accountable rather than target the people’s barricade, which residents put up in response to the company’s activities.

The people of Kasibu have once again demonstrated its steadfast defense of their land after the police withdrew from enforcing the temporary restraining order (TRO) filed by the North Luzon Mineral Resources Corporation (NLMRC) and the Bugkalot Confederation.

On Friday, October 30, the news broke that the police came to the people’s barricade in Kasibu attempting to dismantle it through a court order. This is after the NLMRC and Bugkalot Confederation filed a complaint seeking an injunction and a temporary restraining order to stop residents from maintaining barricades along the roads of Pao, Catawaran, Kakidugen, and Paquet. Once cleared, this would allow the company to proceed with its mining exploration activities.

Rights group Karapatan hailed the withdrawal of the police, saying that the community’s strong resistance against large-scale mining only proved that they are determined to defend their rights and their livelihood.

“Their struggle must be respected, not met with police deployment, threats, arrests, fabricated charges, and legal harassment,” the group said in a statement.

“The enforcement of the temporary restraining order sought by NLMRC must not be used to suppress community resistance and advance corporate mining interests at the expense of the people,” Karapatan stated.

The court order was issued on October 28 by Regional Trial Court Branch 30 Judge Paul Attolba Jr. following a complaint filed by NLMRC and Bugkalot Federation of Nueva Vizcaya against members of the anti-mining community for blocking their mining equipment. The company holds a mining exploration permit covering 4,456 hectares, including ancestral lands, granted by Mines and Geoscience Bureau (MGB) in June 2025.

The anti-mining community asserted that the people’s barricade is legitimate and justified, as residents are only defending their rights, environment and livelihood.

They also questioned the validity of the mining exploration permit, saying it was granted without genuine consultation with the affected communities. Members of the community themselves have experienced the effects of the mining exploration on their community, saying it is affecting their crops and access to clean water.

The Center for Environmental Concerns (CEC) said the TRO reflects how the state treats the environmental defenders and the communities that will be affected by mining exploration activities.

“Rather than criminalizing defenders and putting their lives at risk, the judiciary and local government units must fulfill their mandate to serve the public good, uphold human rights, and environmental protection,“ the CEC said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the Climate Change Network for Community-based Initiatives (CCNCI) accused Attolba Jr. of serving the interest of the mining company instead of the community and the environment.

The group said that the same RTC also issued writ of preliminary injunction against the people’s barricade in Dupax Del Norte against Woggle Corporation’s mining exploration that led to the violent dispersal of the said barricade and unjustly arrested seven residents on January 23 this year.

“The dispersal is a blatant example of the NLMRC’s corporate greed and to the lengths they are willing to go for their own interests – weaponizing legal mechanisms, state-mandated violence, and the destruction of the environment for the sake of their profits that does not benefit local communities,” CCNCI said in their statement.

Since May, the affected community has maintained the barricade, effectively halting NLMRC’s mining exploration activities and causing the company to incur an estimated P8 million ($125, 201) losses.

Alyansa ng Novo Vizcayano para sa Kalikasan (ANVIK) argued that the court should hold NLMRC accountable rather than target the people’s barricade, which residents put up in response to the company’s activities.

“In a desperate attempt to push through their destructive large-scale mining that the community is vehemently rejecting, they colluded with the police to get the NLMRC’s mining equipment inside,” ANVIK said in their statement.

“Aside from NLMRC, their accomplice should be held accountable for allowing the destructive mining to enter our community without proper consultation such as the police, local officials, and to DENR and MGB under the Marcos Jr administration,” ANVIK added.

Kalikasan People’s Network for the Environment (KPNE) called for an independent investigation, as the community seeks for transparency over irregularities on NLMRC’s alleged bogus consultation.

KPNE also questioned whether the agencies involved in harassment and intimidation of the people’s barricade truly serve the people. “Residents have already endured arrests and criminal charges connected to their participation in the barricade,” the group added.

On October 19, ANVIK along with other local environment defenders filed a position paper before the Department of Defense (DND), Department of Energy and Natural Resources (DENR), and MGB to grant their demands.

In the document, they reiterated that both NLMRC and Woggle Corporation bypassed genuine consultation along with the local community. They added that the mining exploration causes irreversible damage to the environment as Nueva Vizcaya is the critical watershed for Cagayan Valley Region.

The document also said that continued operations of both companies have been linked to serious human rights violations as police forces commit violent arrests and even use the laws against the community who are exercising their rights to protect the environment.

Over 31 cases against Indigenous leaders, a priest, and community lawyers have been subjected to Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP) filed by NLMRC since the people’s barricade started.

They demanded immediate cancellation of mining exploration of both mining companies, investigation of the alleged bypassing of consultation, and to strengthen Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) and implementation of laws protecting the environment.

CCNCI also linked the reported violent dispersal attempt to the Ferdinand Marcos Jr. administration’s efforts to fast track mining activities in the Philippines.

The group cited the Mining Fiscal Regime (RA No. 12253) and the implementation of the Critical Minerals Act Executive Order (EO) 122 establishing a framework to develop critical minerals through domestic processing.

KPNE pointed out that this case, along with other cases of people’s resistance against large-scale mining in different parts of Nueva Vizcaya, exposes what it described as the Marcos Jr’s misleading claims of “reliable and responsible mining production.”

Local communities at Kasibu along with environmental groups demanded the NLMRC’s cancellation of mining exploration permit and to hold officials involved in letting a large-scale mining operation without genuine consultation be held accountable. (AMU, RVO)

author: Kalikasan PNE
title: Debt, plunder and disaster
content:
Southern Leyte during the aftermath of Typhoon Odette (Photo by LCDE)

Public money pays for transmission lines, ports, and guarantees, while private firms collect profits for decades. The public absorbs the risk and the debt; the corporations keep the gains.

Every year, typhoons, floods, and landslides batter the Philippines, and every year the same story follows: the country is among the most climate-vulnerable in the world. In recent years, the Marcos Jr. administration’s answer is to borrow from private banks and international financing institutions (IFIs) such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF-WB).

The Philippines contributes very little to the greenhouse gases warming the planet, yet we are forced to take on debt to address a crisis we did not create. The IMF-WB has helped imperialist countries, primarily the United States, shape our economy around debt repayment, raw-material exports, and foreign control. For more than half a century, their intervention has driven the depletion of our natural resources, widespread poverty, and environmental destruction. A real alternative exists, and it begins with cutting our financial dependence on these institutions and breaking US imperialist control over our country.

The Philippines was among the earliest testing grounds for structural adjustment: World Bank loans in 1980 and 1987, and 23 IMF programs between 1962 and 2000. From Marcos Sr. in the 1970s to Marcos Jr. today, the conditionalities of this debt trap have been implemented. Key measures included:

World Bank structural adjustment loans (1980–1987): tariff cuts, import liberalization, and a push toward export-oriented industry.

IMF programs (1980s): peso devaluation and floating, austerity, and prioritizing debt service. Automatic appropriation for debt payments dates back to Marcos-era decrees.

Privatization: the Asset Privatization Trust (1986), the Manila water concessions (1997), and the power sector under Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA) (2001).

Deregulation: Oil industry deregulation (1996–1998) and the Mining Act of 1995.

Investment liberalization: the Foreign Investments Act (1991) and the Build-Operate-Transfer law (1990).

Tax reforms: the Value-Added Tax (VAT) (1988) and its 2005 expansion, both pushed by IMF programs.

The script was consistent: lower or eliminate taxes on foreign and big firms, open our markets to imports and investment, privatize public services, cut public spending, and expand raw-material exports like minerals. The result was an economy kept agrarian, underdeveloped, and reliant on foreign capital.

Also linked to foreign debt is the devaluation of peso which made the situation worse. When the peso drops, our debt in foreign currency increases. To earn dollars, we must export more timber, minerals, and agricultural products, and to entice foreign investment, wages and labor rights must be suppressed. The burden has fallen hardest on landless farmers, fishers pushed out by commercial fleets, upland Indigenous communities, and low-wage workers who keep losing their livelihoods.

The Bataan Nuclear Power Plant shows how foreign debt burdens the people twice. Built under Marcos for roughly $2.3 billion, it never produced a single watt of electricity, yet Filipinos paid for it for decades. When the debt crisis hit in the 1980s, the government automatically allocated its budget to debt repayment while cutting funds for health and education.

Then came the Mining Act of 1995, which allowed 100-percent foreign-owned companies to hold large mining agreements. World Bank documents of the period treated limits on foreign ownership as an obstacle to be removed. Our minerals were extracted and shipped abroad, leaving communities with lost forests, poisoned rivers and seas, mine waste, militarization, and displacement. We never built the heavy industry that could have turned our own minerals into goods and jobs.

Today, the same institutions tell vulnerable countries they must fund climate resilience and clean energy. Since 2021, we have borrowed from the World Bank through disaster loans, policy loans, a community-resilience loan, and energy-transition loans. That adds up to more than $4 billion in under six years, every centavo to be repaid. Civil society research shows that in 2024, nearly 99 percent of climate- and disaster-related assistance came as loans, not grants. The climate crisis and the vulnerability of poor countries have become a business opportunity.

The energy-transition loans came as policy loans, released only when the government enacts reforms: opening renewables to full foreign ownership, creating a renewable energy market, preparing offshore wind auctions, expanding retail competition, and “de-risking” projects for private developers. Public money pays for transmission lines, ports, and guarantees, while private firms collect profits for decades. The public absorbs the risk and the debt; the corporations keep the gains.

We have seen this before. Privatization and deregulation turned electricity into a commodity, and consumers now pay for the profits of giants like Meralco. Applying the same logic to renewables does not make it just. A solar farm can take farmland, an offshore wind zone can lock fishers out of their own waters, and a transmission corridor can uproot a community. Clean energy controlled by corporations is still corporate control, bringing more environmental destruction and higher electricity rates.

The rush for critical minerals like nickel, copper, and cobalt is called “green extractivism”: the same old plunder under a new label. If foreign corporations still own the deposits, the technology, and the market, it is not a transition. Marcos Jr. recently signed an onerous Memorandum of Understanding with US President Donald Trump giving the US and its companies preference over our critical minerals. To hasten the process, he issued Executive Order No. 122, establishing a National Policy Framework for Developing the Critical Minerals Industry and reorganizing the Mining Industry Coordinating Council (MICC) to speed up the extraction, processing, and export of raw minerals.

Corruption is the other face of this dependence. Hundreds of billions of pesos borrowed for flood control, dredging, reforestation, climate mitigation, and disaster prevention often end up in the pockets of vulture officials in local governments, Congress, the Senate, and Malacañang. A government that serves foreign creditors and plunderers at the same time has no reason to serve its people.

I am not against climate action. We urgently need adaptation, renewable energy, ecosystem restoration, and an end to fossil-fuel dependence. But it must be under our own control, which I believe means:

Reversing neoliberal policies: nationalizing basic industries like mining, oil, and power, and repealing the Mining Act of 1995 and the EPIRA Law.

Ending automatic debt appropriations: redirecting most debt-service funds to public services and facilities.

Repudiating odious debts: refusing to repay loans tied to failed or corrupt projects like flood control schemes and megadams.

Climate reparations and disaster compensation, not new debt: loss-and-damage funds as grants, additional to existing aid, reaching communities directly with no privatization strings.

Domestic financing: funding adaptation by taxing fossil-fuel and mining companies, windfall profits, and extreme wealth, not by squeezing the poor.

Democratic energy control: rebuilding the government’s capacity to generate, store, and distribute renewable power, strengthening electric cooperatives, prioritizing rooftop and community solar and microgrids, and guaranteeing lifeline electricity.

Fossil-fuel workers must be assured income, retraining, and decent jobs; a just transition cannot mean replacing regular workers with contractual ones.

These reforms are worth fighting for, but the long-lasting solution lies deeper. We need national industrialization alongside genuine land reform, and ultimately the overturning of this rotten, bankrupt semi-colonial and semi-feudal society. Only then can real environmental rehabilitation begin, with sound use of our natural resources in service of our people’s needs.

The future we must fight for is free from imperialist dictates and plunder. Down with US imperialism!

title: Kapatid seeks probe of jail reservation commercialization
content:
New Bilibid Prison. Screengrab from Google Earth

“We mean protecting 366.7 hectares of public land so it can be transformed into a modern, humanized center for custody, legal aid, and reformation.”

Political prisoners’ support group Kapatid urged Congress to investigate plans to commercialize the New Bilibid Prison (NBP) reservation in Muntinlupa City, warning that the proposed closure of the facility could displace not only inmates but also long-time residents living within its grounds.

Kapatid received reports that some residents got three eviction notices and that hearings were underway. The group called on Congress to include the affected communities in its proposed legislative inquiry and to ensure their welfare and protection.

Kapatid also launched its “Protect Bilibid Lands” campaign, calling for the preservation of the entire NBP reservation as a permanent national correctional center and an immediate halt to plans to close the facility by 2028 and convert its grounds into a commercial real estate venture.

The group urged both chambers of Congress to investigate Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) Director General Gregorio Catapang Jr. ‘s reported moves to commercialize 366.7 hectares of public land identified under Proclamation No. 1159. The area is 52.79% larger than the 240-hectare Bonifacio Global City and is projected to generate P1 billion to P2 billion in annual lease revenues.

“When we say ‘Protect Bilibid Lands,’ we do not mean preserving a broken, corrupt prison system. We mean protecting 366.7 hectares of public land so it can be transformed into a modern, humanized center for custody, legal aid, and reformation,” said Fides Lim, Kapatid spokesperson. “Amid widespread corruption scandals and the lack of accountability, a congressional inquiry is urgently needed to compel full transparency since mass transfers are being used as a pretext for decongestion to empty prime public land for commercial profit.”

Kapatid said that retaining NBP as a national correctional center is necessary to keep prisoners near their families and support their rehabilitation.

Citing BuCor data, the group said that 12,878 of the 21,129 persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) at NBP, or nearly 61%, came from the National Capital Region, CALABARZON and Central Luzon.

The NCR accounted for 5,998 prisoners, or 28.39% of the population, followed by CALABARZON with 4,199 or 19.87%, and Central Luzon with 2,681 or 12.69 percent. Including Bicol’s 2,028 prisoners, Kapatid said that 14,906 PDLs, or 70.55% of the total, came from these four contiguous Luzon regions.

“Retaining NBP ensures that 6 out of every 10 inmates remain near their families for regular visitations which are clinically proven to improve mental health and rehabilitation success,” Lim said.

She also cited Rule 59 of the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, known as the Nelson Mandela Rules which calls for prisoners to be allocated to facilities close to their homes or places of social rehabilitation.

Kapatid warned that transferring prisoners to remote penal colonies would increase travel expenses for low-income families and weaken the family support networks needed during rehabilitation.

The group also cautioned that mass transfers could merely shift overcrowding to other facilities. It cited occupancy rates of 541% at Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm, 504% at Leyte Regional Prison, and 399% at San Ramon Prison in Zamboanga City.

KAPATID further cited 6,538 prisoner deaths across BuCor facilities from 2020 to 2025, warning that separating vulnerable prisoners from their families could worsen the prison health crisis.

The group said that the proposed commercialization must be assessed against Republic Act No. 10575, or the Bureau of Corrections Act of 2013 which establishes BuCor’s responsibilities for the safekeeping and reformation of national prisoners and provides for standard correctional facilities, including hospitals and visiting areas.

Kapatid maintained that decongestion should address systemic problems in the criminal justice system rather than rely on the transfer of prisoners to distant penal colonies.

“Real decongestion requires judicial efficiency and structural reforms, including clearing administrative backlogs that force prisoners who have fully served their sentences to resort to costly habeas corpus petitions for release; releasing elderly and very ill prisoners on humanitarian grounds; and ending the drug war that fuels extreme prison overcrowding,” Lim said.

The group’s campaign builds on a petition submitted to the Department of Justice on July 24 signed by 45 political prisoners at NBP, including 12 senior citizens and 18 people with medical conditions.

The petition opposed forced mass transfers to distant penal colonies and called for human rights safeguards, including prior formal notice and written consent from PDLs.

Kapatid said that preserving the NBP reservation does not mean maintaining the existing prison system unchanged, but transforming the public land into a modern correctional facility that upholds human dignity, access to legal assistance and rehabilitation.

The group called on Congress to investigate the proposed land conversion, ensure transparency in decisions involving public property, and protect both prisoners and long-time residents who could be affected by the planned closure and commercialization of the reservation. (DAA)

title: Farmers reiterate demand for genuine agrarian reform
content:
MANILA — Farmers, fisherfolk along with Indigenous peoples and advocates culminated this year’s Peasant Month on October 21 by marching from España to Mendiola after a week-long camp out, bringing longstanding calls for genuine agrarian reform.

The Super El Niño, land-use conversion and human rights abuses are among the key issues aggravating the plight of rural folk.

Farmers from Southern Tagalog and Central Luzon expressed deep frustration by the state’s suggestion to use buckets to collect water. They decried the lack of government aid like subsidies for the dry spells, leaving many without food to sustain themselves and their families.

Other issues they highlighted are the Pax Silica initiative and various renewable energy projects which will convert their farmland into infrastructure which they said “will serve corporate interests and the US military complex.”

They condemned the continuing U.S. intervention in many aspects of the nation’s affairs. They vowed to hold protest actions on the upcoming visit of U.S. President Donald Trump,or this year’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) forum. (RVO)

title: Pulis
content:
Policemen disperse the protesters in front of the House of Representatives, Sept. 9. (Photo by Jose Santos)

Walang maaasahan sa institusyong hindi nagsisilbi sa interes ng mga nasa laylayan.

Insulto man sa halaman at hayop na hindi hamak na mas may ambag sa pananatili ng kalikasan, naging uso na ang mga terminong pulis patola at pulis buwaya para ilarawan ang kabulukan at kapalpakan ng institusyong dapat na nagsisilbi at nagtatanggol sa mamamayan.

May mga nakaunipormeng wagas kung magpahayag ng kanilang karahasan. Pati mapayapang protesta, pinipigilan. Sinusugod ang barikada. Nang-aaresto nang walang pakundangan. Nanunulak at namamalo ng mga dumadalo sa rally. Walang pakialam kung may humandusay sa kalyeng duguan. Mistulang nawala na ang katinuan dahil sa pagiging utak pulbura.

Sadyang walang pakialam, walang paggalang sa batayang karapatan. Kahit ang mga peryodista, hindi na ligtas sa kalupitan ng pulis. Noong Okt. 19, may peryodistang sinaktan dahil lang nagkober ng protesta ng mga magsasaka sa tapat ng gusali ng Department of Agrarian Reform.

Sinubukan pa siyang arestuhin. Napilitan lang siyang pakawalan dahil napansing maraming nagbibidyo ng nangyari at maraming aktibistang lumalapit para ipaliwanag na peryodista ang kinakaladkad at pinagtutulungan nila.

Nakapagtataka lang na binabaligtad ngayon ng mga pulis ang nangyari. “Initial reports indicate that a verbal altercation occurred involving an individual who identified himself as a member of the media and deployed police personnel. The individual allegedly uttered profane remarks and kicked several police personnel. In response, the officers intervened to prevent further escalation. The individual was subsequently released.”

Kung susuriin ang press release ng mga pulis noong Okt. 20, hindi binanggit na iniwan nilang sugatan ang peryodistang pinagtulungang damputin at kaladkarin. Tila hindi nangyari ang ilang beses na pagsigaw niya ng “Media ako!” habang ipinapakita ang press ID na hindi pinansin ng mga nagbibingi-bingihan at nagbubulag-bulagan.

Basta para sa kanila, may kailangang masampolan para hindi na siya gayahin ng iba pang peryodista. Kahit na hindi nila binanggit ang terminong “chilling effect,” ito pa rin ang nais nilang mangyari para mapatahimik ang midya sa pag-uulat ng mga nangyayari sa lipunan, lalo na sa kanayunan.

Kinikilala at nirerespeto raw ng mga pulis ang kalayaan sa pamamahayag, pati na ang tinatawag nilang “peaceful assembly.” Pero bakit parati silang humihingi ng “permit to rally” para magkaroon ng mga mapayapang pagtitipon? Gayundin ang nangyari sa pagkilos ng mga magsasaka kamakailan. Pinapadaan sa komplikadong burukrasya ang lehitimong pagpapahayag ng saloobin.

Hanggang ngayon, ginagamit pa ring batayan ng represyon ang Batas Pambansa 880 o Public Assembly Act of 1985 na ipinatupad ng diktador na si Ferdinand Marcos Sr. Ito ang dahilan kung bakit napapanahon nang ibasura ang batas na itong sinisikil ang batayang karapatan. Kung totoong naglilingkod sa interes ng mamamayan ang mga pulis, dapat na hinahayaan lang nila ang mga mapayapang pagtitipon at hindi nila pagmamalupitan ang mga nagpoprotesta’t peryodista.

Pero walang maaasahan sa institusyong hindi nagsisilbi sa interes ng mga nasa laylayan. Palibhasa, mas pinapaboran nila ang interes ng mga nasa kapangyarihan. Sadyang may kabulukang nagreresulta sa utak pulburang oryentasyon. Asahang patuloy na lalabanan ang kanilang pandarahas sa mga peryodista’t ordinaryong mamamayan.

Patola na, buwaya pa. Idagdag na rin ang mga salitang marahas at sinungaling. Posible ring tawagin silang kaaway ng kapayapaan. Sa konteksto ng pagpapatuloy ng kanilang masamang gawi, mainam na isang salita na lang ang gamitin. Pasista.

title: Southern Tagalog workers on 45-peso wage hike: ‘Insulting’
content:
The workers reiterated their demand for a P1,200 (US$18.92) national minimum wage.

CABUYAO CITY — Workers in Southern Tagalog denounced the newly approved wage increase of P25 (US$0.39) to P45 (US$0.71) for minimum wage earners, saying the adjustment offers little relief to workers struggling with rising prices of food, fuel, and other basic necessities.

The Alyansa ng mga Manggagawa sa Probinsya ng Laguna (ALMAPILA) and Pagkakaisa ng mga Manggagawa sa Timog Katagalugan – Kilusang Mayo Uno (PAMANTIK-KMU) described the wage adjustment as an insult to workers in Laguna and the rest of Southern Tagalog.

In a protest October 16 outside the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) IV-A office, the Workers’ Initiative for Wage Increase-Southern Tagalog (WIN4WIN-ST) criticized Wage Order No. 23 as insufficient to address the widening gap between wages and the cost of living.

“Workers in CALABARZON have long endured extremely low wages, cutting back on expenses, pawning their ATM cards, getting sick, and going hungry despite their significant contribution to the national economy,” WIN4WIN-ST said in a statement.

title: ‘Release tortured Mangyan organizer’
content:
“He needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.”

Indigenous Mangyan farmer and organizer Miguel Magbata was reportedly beaten and tortured while in military custody after his arrest in Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro, on October 14, prompting human rights groups to call for his immediate release and to hold accountable those responsible.

According to Karapatan Southern Tagalog, Magbata was arrested after a reported armed encounter between the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and alleged New People’s Army (NPA) members in Sitio Badyang, Barangay San Roque in Bulalacao. He was reportedly subjected to physical abuse and interrogation by the 1st Infantry Battalion (IB) under the command of the 203rd Infantry Brigade (IBde).

After days of uncertainty over his whereabouts, reports emerged that Magbata was transferred to Roxas Municipal Police Station. Defend Mindoro said that he needs immediate medical attention for injuries and trauma allegedly sustained during his detention.

The group also raised concerns over a Facebook post from 203rd Infantry Brigade of Philippine Army about Magbata’s children and family, published without their consent, which it said could compromise their safety.

Despite his reported transfer to police custody, the military reportedly sought to retain custody of Magbata. Defend Mindoro demanded his immediate release and called for accountability from the 203rd IBde led by Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo, and the 1st IB, under Lt. Col. Edwin Mirador.

Defend Mindoro said that Magbata’s case shows a pattern of harassment and abuses against Indigenous Peoples, farmers, and community organizers in Mindoro where those asserting their rights are often accused of links to the communist armed movement.

The group cited the killings of Indigenous and peasant individuals Jay-el Maligday, Hulyo Agtay, and Juan Sumilhig which it attributed to military abuses. It also stressed the case of Dolores Solangon, an elderly Mangyan-Iraya woman who reportedly endured illegal arrest and nine hours of torture at the hands of elements from the 76th IB.

Maligday, a young Hanunuo-Mangyan, was allegedly killed by soldiers of the 4th IB while sleeping in his home. The same unit was accused of beating another Hanunuo-Mangyan, Minggo, in Mansalay early this year.

For Defend Mindoro, these abuses are inseparable from the land disputes and economic hardships confronting Indigenous communities and farmers.

In Bulalacao, the group said that large-scale mining and renewable energy projects threaten ancestral lands and local livelihoods. These include developments associated with CleanTech Global Renewables and Singapore-based The Blue Circle which is reportedly planning an offshore wind project involving 100 turbines across a proposed 40,050-hectare area.

Meanwhile, drought has exacerbated the farmers’ hardship. In 2024, an estimated 864 hectares of farmland in Bulalacao were damaged, resulting in P87 million (US$1.37 million) in agricultural losses and affecting around 1,000 registered farmers, according to Defend Mindoro. With another severe El Niño episode looming, communities face renewed threats of crop failure and water shortage.

The group criticized the government for prioritizing counterinsurgency operations over addressing rural poverty, landlessness, and the climate crisis. It said that militarization further endangers communities already struggling to protect their livelihoods and ancestral territories.

Defend Mindoro demanded an independent investigation into the allegations of torture and illegal detention. Torture is prohibited under international law and civilians must be protected from violence and cruel treatment in situations of armed conflict.

The group held the 203rd IBde and the Marcos Jr. administration accountable for the alleged violations, calling for an end to military harassment of Indigenous Peoples and farmers.

For Defend Mindoro, Magbata’s case underscores the dangers faced by community organizers defending the rights of rural communities. “No allegation of insurgency can justify torture or the denial of due process,” the group wrote in a statement. (DAA)

title: Farmers decry government’s lack of preparation for Super El Niño
content:
Farmers, scientists and environmentalists, held a forum, October 18 on the impacts of Super El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk and the government’s lack of preparations for it.

A Super El Niño is a stronger El Niño where the temperature of the Pacific Ocean increases to 2C above the average. In the Philippines, it leads to the extreme shifting of weather conditions, bringing in severe drought, or stronger rainfall events. For farmers, it is the government’s unpreparedness that turns it into an even greater calamity, made even worse by the climate crisis.

Farmers Geraldine Patriarca and Ginny Nabia from Bicol and Negros expressed how their communities are already experiencing extreme drought, and are unable to sustain themselves and their families. They demanded Marcos Jr. to give genuine solutions to farmers’ struggles, not his proposed buckets that they say “will barely even catch any rain.”

Irish Cuaresma of Advocates of Science and Technology for the People (Agham), added that farmers and Indigenous peoples are further undermined by “disaster capitalism,” where corporations benefit from humanitarian crises.

Sharl Lopez of Philippine Network of Food Security Programs (PNFSP) meanwhile, criticized the government for not upholding their obligation to uphold the people’s right to food security, and advocated for the passing of the Right to Adequate Food Bill.

author: Anne Marxze Umil
title: Int’l solidarity vs Pax Silica
content:
At the Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder workshop in Bangkok, Thailand on October 14, 2026. (Photo from ILPS Philippines Facebook page)

Despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance.

BANGKOK – Organizations from different parts of the world are now united against the Pax Silica Initiative to be signed by the United States and the Philippines in November. US President Donald Trump reportedly will visit the Philippines to sign the agreement.

“We are in a period of extreme conflict between two very powerful and imperialist countries and the US is trembling and shaking. We have to maintain that fervor of revolution, that ability to throw stones at them, to bring them down and to make sure that the US imperialist power is no more,” said Azra Sayeed, secretary-general of the International League of Peoples Struggles (ILPS) during an activity in Bangkok, Thailand dubbed “Shut the Pax Down: Resistance and Solidarity Against Imperialist Plunder” on October 14.

The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank (IMF-WB) held its annual meeting in Bangkok from October 12 to 18. Participants included central bank governors, economic policy makers and business leaders.

In a statement, the Campaigners of the Peoples Global Campaign (PGC) Against IMF and World expressed concern over IMF-WB’s push for new technologies, including the widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in Global South economies.

The group said that the “frantic race” for AI dominance intensified mining and extraction in resource-rich countries in the Global South. Transnational corporations are extracting rare earth elements (REEs) and other critical minerals to meet the growing demand for AI infrastructure. To secure control over the AI supply chain, countries like the US initiated the formation of Pax Silica and other similar formations.

“We know that imperialism is about world domination and control over resources. In the previous century, the rivalry among imperialist powers centered on oil because whoever controlled oil could wield significant influence over the military and the economy,” Arnold Padilla, secretary-general of ILPS-Philippines said during the event.

Now, he stressed, the battle is over critical minerals as whoever controls AI and the critical minerals needed to build its infrastructure could gain a significant advantage in dominating the world. “Essentially, that’s the battle now between the US and China. So, who will control this critical sector?”

This is why, Padilla said, the Philippines is up for a major battle to halt the signing of the US-led Pax Silica Initiative this year in time for the Asean Summit from November 16 to 18.

He said that AI is not just about the software that people use but also about weapons like drones “that can make decisions in actual battles without any human intervention.” He added that these sophisticated weapons will be made of minerals to be extracted from the Philippines.

Read: Critical minerals policy framework linked to Pax Silica? Read: War and plunder: US imperialism in the Philippines

“Pax Silica is made up of 24 countries, of course, led by the US. And it’s a special coalition. Specifically chosen by the US because countries that belong to Pax Silica perform a specific specialized role because it’s about controlling the supply chain,” Padilla said. “We don’t have high technology, we don’t have the logistic network, we don’t have capital or energy. But what do we have? We have the critical minerals. So for us in the Philippines, this is all about plunder.”

Donna Denina, secretary-general of International Women’s Alliance (IWA), said that US Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, former tech executive and adviser tied to the controversial software firm Palantir, designed Pax Silica to give the US control over the global technology supply chain.

Palantir is a technology firm with clients from the Pentagon and foreign militaries including the Israeli government. But Denina said that Palantir is now expanding its influence beyond military tech into the health care sector.

In the US, she said that Palantir’s AI software is being used to manage hospital staffing and scheduling. This raised concerns among healthcare workers and prompted protests.

She said that more than 1,000 nurses from the National Nurses United union protested against healthcare institutions’ contracts with Palantir. “They are concerned that AI systems could replace human decision-making in the hospital. Nurses warn that relying on AI could reduce human oversight in decisions affecting patients’ care and well-being.”

She stressed that Palantir’s expansion in the United Kingdom’s National Health Service (NHS) was also protested by patients, health workers and the public.

Denina said that with the expansion of AI requires large data centers that consume vast amounts of land and water. She said that this is why some US states and cities banned or restricted the construction of data centers.

According to Data Center Watch, $64 billion of data center projects have been blocked or delayed due to local opposition.

“So not only is Palantir trying to monopolize war technology, it’s now expanding into health technology and trying to dominate AI tech firms to win contracts. And they suspect that Palantir will be the number one beneficiary for the Pax Silica agreement because of the types of technologies they can offer,” Denina said.

She added that despite the advancements of AI technology, there is also the growing resistance. “I think people in the US understand the impacts of the Pax Silica Agreement.”

“To support and facilitate more AI technology, there’s going to be more public funding spent on government contracts to support AI technology. Public spending that could be used towards supporting the local communities,” Denina said, adding that Bagong Alyasang Makabayan (Bayan) US chapter launched the Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network last September was joined by Filipino Americans in the US and other nationalities.

Read: US-wide campaign against Pax Silica launched

Sayeed called on different nations to show resistance against the US whose President is set to come to the Philippines next month.

“I recall reading Joma (Jose Maria Sison). He states that imperialism and feudalism are man-made social phenomena which are to exploit and oppress the people. They are plunderers of both humans and nature,” Sayeed said, adding that critical minerals are key to the industrial military complex as well.

This is why, she said, the US is trying to get hold of the supply chain. She said that the Philippines and Indonesia have critical minerals.

“We must all show up to make sure that he knows Asia. Whether we are in the Philippines or Indonesia or Pakistan or Nepal or India, we have to say, ‘you are not welcome,’” Sayeed said.

“Our resistance has to be fueled by the pain of the people. We fight for our people, we fight for our land, we fight for our destiny. So, that is who we are. And we will not forget.That come 16th of November, when he comes, he will be told you are not welcome across Asia and the Pacific. Let’s make this across Asia and the Pacific, not only the Philippines,” she added. (DAA)

title: Mindanao beverage firm workers denounce unequal treatment
content:
Having equal pay is what we are after because we are delivering the same [products].

For months, workers have been demanding an end to a multinational beverage corporation’s alleged unequal treatment of its workforce in Mindanao.

The Samahan ng Manggagawa sa Coca-Cola (SAMACOKE) and Nagkakaisang Manggagawa ng Buong Lohistika at Distribusyon ng Coca-Cola Southern at Central Mindanao (NMLDCC-SCM), both affiliated with the Federation and Cooperation of Cola, Beverage, and Allied Industry Unions (FCCU), have been in negotiations with Coca-Cola Europacific Aboitiz Philippines (CCEAP) for a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) to have equal benefits and wage hikes as their Luzon counterparts.

Edmond*, a Davao City resident and who has been in the company for decades, told Bulatlat that a major concern is the alleged unfair implementation of parameters for workers’ performance incentives. He said that they need to accomplish three certain parameters but this was allegedly not similar to a manufacturing site based in Luzon which requires only one parameter.

“The situation has been reversed. We are the vintage [plant], and we are given parameters that are difficult to achieve,” he said in the vernacular.

Receiving an average P1,500 (US$23.79) of monthly incentive, Edmond said, goes a long way for workers given the increasing prices of basic goods.

Coca-Cola truck drivers in Mindanao, on the other hand, are pushing for an equal reload rate as their Luzon counterparts. Adrian*, who is also a Davao City resident and has been working as a delivery truck driver for the company for more than a decade, said that they get paid P135 (US$2.14) per reload which is too low compared to the supposed reload rate of P265 (US$4.20) in a Coca-Cola manufacturing site in Luzon.

“Having equal pay is what we are after because we are delivering the same [products],” Adrian said in the vernacular.

A reload refers to the second and succeeding delivery of Coca-Cola products to various stores after the first trip. Delivery truck drivers, Adrian said, considered it as their overtime pay.

Both unions also pushed for a P50 (US$0.79) daily wage hike, the same amount allegedly granted to the employees working at the same Luzon-based manufacturing site in 2023. In that year, Edmond said that they were forced to accept the offer of a P40 (US$0.63) increase in daily salary after the provision of other benefits which were also essential for them.

Their last CBA expired in October 2025 but the formal negotiations for a new bargaining agreement started in April this year after it got delayed. As of this writing, both parties have yet to conclude negotiations.

The United Coca-Cola Logistics Employees Association of North Mindanao (UCLEANMINDA-FCCU), covering workers from Misamis Oriental and the cities of Iligan, Butuan, and Zamboanga, is facing a separate issue as the company allegedly refused to bargain.

Jasper Mabuloc, UCLEANMINDA-FCCU president, said that their union was certified as the sole and exclusive bargaining agent (SEBA) of the employees in July. But he said that the company allegedly could not proceed with the negotiation since there was a petition filed by the previous labor union—which allegedly opposed having an election—before the secretary of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE).

The CBA of the previous labor union was also until 2028. “The appeal made by the previous labor union was being used to delay the negotiations,” Mabuloc told Bulatlat in the vernacular. “New union, new CBA.”

Like the NMLDCC-SCM members, the union of Mabuloc also echoed the call for equal reload pay for delivery truck drivers in Mindanao.

Coca-Cola workers have been doing peaceful demonstrations outside their workplace, putting protest banners to voice out their concerns. SAMACOKE is also planning to file a complaint to DOLE after some of their banners were recently taken down by unidentified individuals.

“There should be no disparity because according to what they have said, they nationalized and standardized the implementation of their programs. They should follow,” Edmond said in the vernacular.

Bulatlat reached out to the Coca-Cola company through email on October 18, seeking comments on the alleged disparity of pay and benefits. There was no response as of this posting.

SAMACOKE and NMLDCC-SCM already filed notices of strike. If the company does not have an appropriate response to their demands, Edmond and Mabuloc said that they do not have a choice but to launch a work stoppage. (DAA)

“We left the Philippines with our hopes and dreams. With the desire for a better future for our families, we took risks working in different countries,” one of the workers said.

Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of the Kalipunan ng Katutubong Mamamayan ng Pilipinas (Katribu), soeaks during a forum on October 6, 2026. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat

“Energy transition should be an opportunity to develop our self-sufficiency in manufacturing, engineering, and research.”

ASEAN’s energy future is being planned at a forum filled with representatives from corporations, government, banks, and international institutions. Those from grassroots communities are nowhere to be found.

The ASEAN Energy Business Forum was held in Manila from October 5 to 9, bringing more than 1,500 high-level delegates and officials.

“The forum speaks sweetly about innovation, investment, sustainable energy future: identifying projects to fund and profit from,” said Sonny Africa, executive director of think-tank Ibon Foundation, during a parallel conference. “For ordinary people, the essence is not defined by the amount of investments, bankable projects, public-private partnerships, energy companies, and financing but the simplest questions: is the electricity cost lower? Is it more efficient and more accessible?”

The Philippines is assuming the ASEAN chairpersonship this year. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said that the government will use the opportunity to champion “immediate energy security with long-term resilience.”

title: Progressives renew solidarity with Palestinian resistance
content:
MANILA – Progressive formations led by Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), and International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines marched toward the US embassy on the third year since the Al-Aqsa flood. They condemned U.S., Israel and its allies for the continued genocide of Palestine and military aggression on West Asia.

The Al Aqsa Flood refers to the October 7, 2023 attacks led by Hamas that followed Palestine’s long history of resistance against Israel colonial rule and occupation.

For progressives, the Al-Aqsa Flood is not what the west would label as “terrorist attacks” but rather an act of resistance similar to the Philippines, rooted in decades of oppression and colonialism by imperialist nations like the U.S. and Israel. For PPFA, it is the “beacon to our own resistance… It inspires all people struggling for national and social liberation, and therefore, we must support their resistance as if it were our own.”

By the end of the program, progressives burned the flags of U.S. and Israel, calling to stop the genocide, and reaffirming to fight for genuine freedom and the downfall of Imperialism.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Badoy red tags UP Rural High School teacher, community
content:
A teacher and the community of UP Rural High School are the recent targets of red-tagging by former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) spokesperson Lorraine Badoy.

On October 6, Badoy red-tagged UP Rural High School teacher Trist’n Buenaflor. Before this, Badoy, in a series of Facebook posts, also red-tagged faculty members and students of the UP Rural High School after the UP Day Remembrance of Martial Law.

The UP Rural High School released a statement on October 1, condemning the red-tagging by Badoy and a military agent named “Emjay Chico.”

“We believe in developing learners who can think critically and engage with the complex problems confronting Philippine society and affecting their basic rights to education, decent life, and human dignity,” the statement reads. “It is deeply concerning that a legitimate educational activity and those who participated in it have been subjected to red-tagging.”

The University asserts the right to academic freedom: fostering discourse that is open, informed, and grounded in evidence.

For his part, Buenaflor has stood his ground.

“All I can say is that I love teaching, and I deeply value my university. I am not afraid,” Buenaflor told Bulatlat in an interview. “I will continue my studies and continue teaching and serving society. I will keep moving forward.”
